utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. May I ask the Prosecution to introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin and Ekkehard Withopf, with Kimberly Fleming, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Mirna Milanovic, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Mr. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber wishes to greet all persons present, representatives of the Prosecution, members of the Defence teams, the accused, and all the others present in this courtroom. We have one witness today who will be testifying. But before we hear the witness, there are two problems we have to deal with. First of all, our ruling regarding the reply of the Defence concerning the admission of certain facts from three other cases. And the Chamber, after having deliberated yesterday following the oral request of the Defence, authorises the Defence to produce a reply to the response of the Prosecution. And in order to do so, we give you a time period of one week. You have seven days to produce that reply. And, of course, we will make our ruling after receiving that reply from you. That is the first problem, which we have resolved in the manner indicated. The second outstanding issue has to do with the request made by the Chamber yesterday regarding the list of documents which were given to the expert military witness. In this connection, the Chamber wishes to recall that before the beginning of the trial a list of documents produced by the Prosecution and disclosed to the Defence was agreed upon. After that, a new list with some new witnesses was also proposed by the Prosecution, and this new list of documents that could become exhibits once tendered into evidence were also agreed upon. Having studied in detail the mentioned documents which were given to the expert witness, that is, General Reinhardt, it appears in fact that he had in his possession 107 documents numbered 1 to 107, 108 being his final report. And also, there was a list of additional documents which figure in Annex B. Therefore, the witness had in his possession 107 documents plus all those appearing in Annex B. In order to have an exhaustive review of all the documents in the possession of this expert witness, I ask the Prosecution to provide us with a recapitulation covering all the documents given to the expert witness, numbering those documents in a numerical order starting from the lowest PT to the highest PT number, and to specify in that list which are the documents that were already on the list that was approved by the Pre-Trial Judge before the opening of the case and which are the documents which were produced as supplementary documents subsequently. I wish to remind the parties - that is, the Prosecution and the Defence - that the documents referred to are, legally, documents which can become exhibits only once during the proceedings they are tendered into evidence at the request of one of the parties - in this case, it will be the Prosecution - and once the document is tendered, the registrar gives it as exhibit number if it is admitted, which mean that the numbers appearing on the Prosecution documents as PT X are only reference numbers of the Prosecution, because there will be a final numbering of those documents which will be provided by the registrar. And I wanted to make that clarification to avoid any confusion. I ask the Prosecution to prepare such a list as soon as possible. I don't think that will be too complicated, because as you know, we have to make a ruling on Exhibit 108, that is, the report. And in order to make a ruling on document 108, we must have this list which would recapitulate the documents mentioned before the beginning of trial, the supplementary documents agreed upon, so that we should know exactly which documents we are talking about. Because as both the Defence and the Prosecution and the Chamber have noted, the expert witness in his preliminary report referred in footnotes to those mentioned documents. For the report to be legible and easily used during the examination and cross-examination, it is necessary to have clearly indicated in the footnotes the numbers that will refer to the -- and that will correspond to the final list that will be drawn up. Mr. Withopf, have you understood the request of the Chamber regarding this list? Which is not complicated, I'm sure, and I hope that we'll be able to have it at the beginning of next week. Mr. Withopf, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. President, I certainly agree with what you have just said. On the 10th of October, we filed the pre-trial brief with the annexed exhibit list. We filed a motion later on in late December to amend the exhibit list, and we detailed that the first 107 out of the 130 exhibits -- proposed exhibits on the supplementary list are such documents the Prosecution has provided its military expert with. We filed on the 23rd of December a further filing, namely, a reply to a Defence response to Prosecution motion to amend the exhibit list. And as you mentioned, Mr. President, in Annex B we attached the consolidated List of Documents provided to General Reinhardt. From this list, it is obvious that the Prosecution provided its military expert many more documents as the ones as listed in the supplementary list. The military expert of the Prosecution received several hundreds of documents, and we will be able to comply with the request by the Chamber at the beginning of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In response to what my learned friend said, on behalf of the Defence, we can confirm that we have indeed received a consolidated list of all the documents given to the expert suggested by the Prosecution, Dr. Reinhardt. We also received from the Prosecution a copy of all those documents which consist of a series of binders. So that we have all the necessary material to prepare the cross-examination of the expert if so decided by the Chamber. All the documents which were given to the experts are a part of the consolidated lists of all the PTs, which the Prosecution intends to tender into evidence in the course of these proceedings. And following what I noted -- what I said yesterday, concerning the videos that we viewed yesterday, I told the Chamber that we would check because we didn't know whether those videos figured on the list -- on the PT lists which the Prosecutor intended to produce. And we did check, and the video did indeed figure on the list of documents which was provided to us by the Prosecution. Nevertheless, Mr. President, I should like to go back to an issue because to this day we are lacking this consolidated list of all the PTs, all the documents which the Prosecutor intends to produce during the trial. We have the initial list of the 10th of October, two or three additional documents given to us either in accordance with the pre-trial brief, and then there are also documents -- additional documents. We have all the documents for the general, but we still do not have a consolidated list of all the documents, and such a list would be very useful for us; that is, a list that would cover all the documents that the Prosecution intends to produce at trial. We have spoken to the Prosecution. They have promised to provide us such a list. And we hope that they will indeed do so as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the Defence for their comments intended to inform the Judges and the participants in this legal debate. It is true that in semantics one must make a distinction between a list of documents and a list of exhibits. The documents become exhibits only once they have been admitted by the Chamber as exhibits and are given an appropriate number. Therefore, quite rightly, the Defence would like to have a complete list, a comprehensive list of the documents which the Prosecution envisages to produce and tender, which doesn't mean to say that all the documents appearing on that list will indeed be tendered and admitted. Therefore, among all the documents referred to so far, they may all be produced, but maybe some will not, and of course it is up to the Prosecution to request the admission of documents when they consider it necessary. For the debate to be fruitful and for all of us to save time, it would be desirable to have a general list of documents which the Prosecution wishes to produce or tender into evidence. Maybe there could even be a blank column which could be filled in once a final exhibit number is given, which would allow us easily to follow the progress made with the admission of documents. Then this list could have an internal Prosecution number, that is, the numbers 00, et cetera, ERN number, then a PT number, and then a blank column which will as the proceedings develop be filled in with the exhibit numbers once they have been admitted into evidence. I think it would be -- this would be useful for the Prosecution, for the Defence, and of course useful for the Judges. I take advantage of the opportunity to ask both the Prosecution and the Defence that when parties intend to tender documents, important documents as exhibits, either Prosecution or Defence exhibits, that when they are official documents - those documents in most cases will be in B/C/S, perhaps some in English - but I cannot emphasise sufficiently that if we have a B/C/S document, a document translated into English, and a document translated into French. Because as you know, when a document is tendered - this may apply just to one paragraph, but it would be better to have the totality of the document - and if the document is originally in the B/C/S, it will of course be entirely translated into English, but it would be desirable to have it translated into French as well. Therefore, an important document that is tendered into evidence, if the document was originally in B/C/S, it should be translated into English and into French to allow the Chamber to fully appreciate the probative value, the relevance, and weight of the document. Because as you know, those documents are produced in the course of the examination-in-chief, sometimes, as we saw yesterday and the day before, there were ten documents produced at the same time. And if all the documents are in B/C/S and then also in English, for the Chamber to be able to quickly evaluate them they should also be translated into French to the extent possible, of course. I hope we have understood each other. Documents that are originally in B/C/S should be translated into English and French. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should simply like to inform the Chamber that the representatives of the Defence have just come from a meeting with representatives of the Registrar regarding the subject of translations. We are still having some difficulties in this connection. Since the last intervention of the Chamber in December, we held several meetings with representatives of the Registrar. A few minutes ago we made a suggestion, a practical suggestion and which would be economical for the Tribunal, which would allow us to always have the documents at least in English for the cross-examination. We fully understand the concern of the Chamber to have those documents in French. We will do our best to have those documents in French as well. But there is a question of resources, which are a major constraint. We have informed the representatives of the Registrar that we would like to have a written response to our request so that the decision that will be taken by the Registrar can be passed on to the Chamber if certain difficulties persist. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor, Mr. Withopf, in a minute. But concerning this problem that we are all well aware of, I wish to tell both to indicate to the Registrar the documents that will be admitted into evidence or tendered into evidence. By way of example: Two days ago, regarding a particular witness, there was a series of documents that were produced and admitted. There were documents that were more or less important. But it was possible for the Defence to take, for example, one document - there was a judgement - to have the body of it translated into French, not more than that. At least this applies to the important documents. Later on, during the proceedings, when we have a military expert and others, and if there's a document that has to do with rules of discipline, the status of officers, the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera, those documents are important and, of course, they deserve to be translated. It's up to both sides to judge the relevance of the documents. And if at your level you're unable to have them translated, you tell the Registrar that these documents are going to be tendered and they need to be translated into both languages to be able to used in the courtroom. Mr. Withopf -- because otherwise the problem of marking documents for identification and then we have to wait. And to avoid this problem, it is best to have all the documents ready at the moment the witness appears -- I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my learned colleague from the Defence side has already addressed the issue of resources. The Prosecution intends to tender into evidence hundreds - hundreds - of documents, documents which consist quite often not only of one page but voluminous documents consisting of tens of pages. We are talking about the translation of thousands of pages of documents into French. As already indicated in the earlier stages of these proceedings, our resources are stretched -- are already stretched to the absolute maximum. To have such documents and even only the important documents - and the Prosecution considers most, at least the vast majority of its documents as important documents - to have them translated into French would cause a serious - a serious - delay in the proceedings. I have, unfortunately -- also I have an understanding for the concern of the Trial Chamber, but realistically, I cannot at this point promise that the Prosecution will translate the documents into French. It would cause a serious problem, and it would most likely cause a delay in the proceedings. This is the situation that both Defence counsel and the Prosecution are facing. I understand Defence has actually a serious problem to get the documents being translated into English. To request from both parties to in addition get such documents being translated into French - and I really think we need to have a realistic view - this would stretch the resources to the -- to an extent which we cannot cope with. Unfortunately, I have to say this, but I wish to have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has taken note of your remarks. You are telling us that there are hundreds of thousands of pages or thousands of documents. It's not a question of the number of pages or thousands of documents. The point is that certain documents have a crucial value; others have a lesser value. And it is up to us to have a hierarchy of documents according to the value or significance attached to those documents. Let us take an example. Let us take a five-page document. Clearly all the paragraphs on this five-page document are not of equal importance. There may be one or two paragraphs on those five pages of importance. Let us in that case translate one or two paragraphs, not the five pages. Clearly, among the thousands of documents we can't ask you to translate all those documents. But when a document is being tendered, everyone knows the importance attached to a particular sentence, a phrase, or a paragraph. Then it would be useful for that particular paragraph to be translated. Because when a witness comes to testify, and on the basis of his testimony a document is produced, this will not be 1.000 pages. It may refer to one or two paragraphs of a written document. And what he will say, which may be important, will be referring to a particular paragraph of a particular document, and it is that paragraph that it would be useful to have. Therefore, both parties should produce a hierarchy of documents and indicate an underlined sentence in B/C/S or English. Instead of it being underlined simply, let it be translated into French, the part that otherwise would be just underlined. That isn't all that complicated. Of course, if there's no other way, then produce your documents in English. But as the majority of the documents will be in B/C/S, or at least a large portion, those documents are translated into English. I might say, "Why in English? Why not in French?", as both languages are official languages. It is up to the Prosecution to establish an equilibrium, a balance between the two languages. Certainly the documents that are in English and are produced by the Prosecution in English, the accused and Defence counsel need to have them in B/C/S. So clearly, those have to be translated into B/C/S for the benefit of the Defence. We'll see as we proceed. But this problem has been raised a long time ago already. Let us now proceed with the hearing of the next witness. I'm going to ask the usher to bring the witness into the courtroom. And until he comes, can the Prosecution tell us whether the witness who has been held up by the snow will be here tomorrow, because the snow hasn't stopped falling since yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is unfortunately the case. The witness has been transported from Sarajevo to Zagreb yesterday. The latest information I got prior to this court session is the following: The witness was still in Zagreb. Due to the weather conditions, flights have been delayed. It's not yet determined as to whether the witness will arrive today or not. I will keep both the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel posted in respect to the further developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a daily flight. If a flight is cancelled, in that case he can only take the flight on the next day; is that right? There's only one flight a day?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are a number of flights and a number of different connections between Zagreb and Amsterdam. The fact that a flight has been delayed or has been cancelled doesn't exclude the possibility that the witness can take a different flight. So there is still some hope that the witness can be presented tomorrow. I may actually get to know in the course of the today's court proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, do you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been invited to give your testimony on behalf of the Prosecution. In order to do that, you're going to give us your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milenko Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6th of February, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in Olovo Ponor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a tradesman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I currently reside in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you give your testimony, you have to take a solemn declaration. Can you please read the text that the usher is giving to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I already indicated, you are here on the invitation of the Prosecution to talk about the facts that took place in 1993. Prosecution is going to ask you certain questions. Can you please answer as completely as possible. If you don't understand a question, you can always ask the person who has put the question to you to rephrase it. After having replied to the questions put to you by the Prosecution - the Prosecution is seated on your right - then the Defence, on your left, is also going to ask you some questions. And also, the three Judges, who are in front of you, can at any moment ask you some questions to clarify things. As you have declared that you will speak the truth and nothing but the truth, I have to tell you that false testimony may be penalised. It may happen that a witness may be asked to answer a question that may bring charges upon him. In that case, the witness is allowed to inform the Chamber that he's not going to answer this question because of that. And in that case the Chamber is going to guarantee such a witness that his answer cannot be used against him, that he will not be able to be incriminated based on his answer. If such a thing happens during your testimony, please tell us that. I will now give the floor to the Prosecution, who are going to start their examination-in-chief. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Ms. Henry-Benjamin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, could you tell the Trial Chamber if you're known by another name, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. People call me Pobro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell the Trial Chamber which municipality your birthplace is located in, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The municipality of Olovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, in 1966, when I served my compulsory military service in Bitola.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you serve?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: For a year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever become a member of any other army? Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992 -- to be more precise, on the 1st of May, I became a member of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you serve in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I served until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from the 1st of May, 1992, when you joined the BH Army, were you on the front lines up until 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I was in a detachment. The name of this detachment was Korita. Later on the 126th Mountain Brigade was formed, and I was assigned to it up to the 15th of December, 1993. And later on I did not any have assignment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Borovcanin, you told us that you served up until the 15th of December, 1993 actively. During that time when you were a member of the -- an active member, that is, of the ABiH, could you tell us what unit you belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I belonged to the Korita Detachment from the very beginning. That was the Territorial Defence of Ilijas municipality. That was up to the establishment of the corps, and that is of the 126th Mountain Brigade. And I had a war assignment up to the 15th December 1993. Then I was said I was too old to be assigned to any war unit; however, I was a volunteer, and a volunteer cannot lose his assignment. And in addition to that, I was not older than 60 at that time, and I was still considered to be an able-bodied man. I lost my assignment. I remained in the army, but I did not have an assignment. And then I received a decision by the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at the time when you were in active service, the 126th Brigade, under whose command did it come?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The 126th Brigade was under the command of the 1st Corps, but it was in the operational zone of the 3rd Corps in the view of the area where it operated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who at that time was the 1st Corps responsible to in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I apologise. I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To put it simply, who did the 1st Corps report to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The 1st Corps reported to the Supreme Command or to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the 3rd Corps responsible for the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: In my opinion, it should not have been, but they coordinated their activities. Given the fact that our brigade was in that territory together with the units of the 3rd Corps, in that area the 3rd Corps was the most important military body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Borovcanin, could you tell the Trial Chamber who was the commander of the 3rd Corps at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: First it was Mr. Alagic and then Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber where you resided from July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: My family resided in Kakanj, in Povezice. And I would occasionally visit them when I was on leave for seven or ten days. I would then come to Kakanj, and I stayed there. Povezice is the name of the street, but also the name of that neighbourhood in the town of Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Trial Chamber if there was any other building on that street that you're aware of.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Across the road from my house was the Sretno Motel. The only thing that separated my house from that hotel was an embankment, a railway embankment. The distance is about 70 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, kindly inform the Trial Chamber what you know of the 18th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I had arrived two days earlier from the front line. I was at home. I came in a caddy vehicle which was mine, but it had been requisitioned by my brigade. I was on a leave, as I've said, and on that day in the late afternoon I saw some vehicles and some troops arriving in front of the Sretno Motel. Truth be told, I was surprised to see that because sometimes I would see military police in various vehicles. This time I don't know what kind of troops were in these vehicles. Their arrival surprised me. At first I thought that this was Mr. Hadzihasanovic's escorts, because up to that time Mr. Hadzihasanovic did not have any escorts. I would see him on two or three occasions. I saw him because his house was maybe three or four houses away from mine. However, due to the conflicts that had been going on in Central Bosnia between Croats and the BH Army, I thought that maybe since there was already the Croatian Defence Council and the Croatian police that for his personal safety he now was escorted by bodyguards. Later on I heard singing and music coming from the motel, and that is all that I saw on that day as I was standing nearby. On the following day I went to the centre of the town of Kakanj. I went for a walk, and I was supposed to collect some food from the Red Cross office. I saw a van was on patrol. Its door was open, and there were some armed people sitting and shouting from the van. I also noticed that some coffee bars were being closed and people were saying, "These men are members of the MOS." They were afraid that something would happen to them and that's why they were closing their establishments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, were you able to see these men? And if you were, could you describe what you saw for us. How did they look physically?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: They wore uniforms. Some wore military blouses; some wore camouflage uniforms. They wore bandannas around their heads. They were armed. Later on one van stopped by a petrol station. There were three soldiers inside and two Mujahedins. They had darker coloured skin. They had beards. They looked Arabic to me. They had white shirts and camouflage uniforms. They didn't have military blouses. And these two men also had knives. I was standing by the shop. Across the road is a small petrol station, a little bit higher from that shop. I was standing with a friend of mine, who said to me -- when I asked him, "What is this MOS doing here in Kakanj," he told me, "Let's split. This doesn't look good. Whenever MOS comes into town, there will be operations. MOS are sabotage units. They didn't come just like that. They must have a reason to be here." I started walking home. When I arrived home --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Did you later that afternoon go back home? Did you return to your home later that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what -- if you did anything, and what?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I said to my wife that something was wrong and to be on the safe side, that she should pack our bags. And I also told a friend of mine, who was also my neighbour - his child had died in Zenica - I asked him if he could watch some of my things. Those were not very valuable things. I took them as I was fleeing my village. And he told me that my things would be safe with him. At dusk, I looked -- actually, I heard some noise coming from the motel. And from the motel, two groups of MOS members started walking across the embankment. One was walking to the left, right from my house; and the other group was on their way towards Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. -- sorry to interrupt you, Witness, but you say that you saw two groups of men, MOS. Could you tell us how you know that these were MOS.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, I knew that they were in the motel, and I knew it was them. And I could see them, because this is not far from where I was, maybe 20 or 30 metres away from my house. They wore bandannas and some had insignia on their arms, and some had green bandannas around their heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you continue. Tell us what transpired, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: This group, which was to my right, stopped in a little meadow, in a little opening. I looked and I saw Mr. Hadzihasanovic, who was talking to them. I couldn't hear what he was saying. I could only see him just -- I ran outside. I took the ABiH registration plates that one normally puts on the car. There was a garage there, and I parked my car there and I covered it with a camouflage cover so that they wouldn't know that this was an ABiH army car. When I looked, the second time I could no longer see Mr. Hadzihasanovic. I could only see a couple of soldiers taking two civilians, who were not tied, and at gunpoint they were taking them towards the Sretno Motel. Within a space -- the space of a couple of minutes, two more civilians were brought in the same direction. At that moment, I could hear a burst of fire from a machine-gun. And a few minutes later I saw that one soldier was carrying a pair of boots in his hand. The others asked him, "What happened?" And then this lad replied, "Foolish guy. He started shooting towards the concrete floor and he wounded himself," and he says, "Give me a car." And then their van came by and those people who were in the van asked what had happened. They repeated the same story. They got into the van and went towards the place from which the burst of fire had been heard, and they left me alone. They didn't take my car, which originally they were going to take. Later on I was not allowed to move about. Nobody was moving about. At a window of the Sretno Motel, there was a sniper. I didn't know what was going on. I thought that these were deserters, but usually when people deserted they would be brought by the military policemen of their own unit. And if -- so I wasn't clear what was going on. I knew that there was something happening, but I didn't know why -- what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw what you thought appeared to be a sniper, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I just didn't dare leave my house. But I asked a woman who lived next to me, because Tone Baric was there with his family. He was the deputy commander of the detachment. I asked her - I didn't dare go myself - I asked her to go and ask Tone what this was all about. And she indeed went there, and when she returned she told me that Tone had been arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon hearing that Tone was arrested, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Then I decided -- it was already the time of curfew. I said to my wife that something major was happening. I didn't want to scare her. I didn't want to scare my child. I thought that this must have been a mistake, because he was the deputy commander. So I said to my wife that I would go and see Mr. Hadzihasanovic to tell him about the mistake that had been made. I did try to do that. On the following morning, I went in that direction where Mr. Hadzihasanovic's house was. And in front of one house I saw a table and there was a soldier sitting there. I didn't see Mr. Hadzihasanovic. On the table, in front of the soldier there was a leather briefcase that officers usually carry. It was my briefcase, the briefcase that I had given as a present to Tone. And I also gave Commander Mirso a torchlight. He had already had a briefcase, so I gave him a torchlight. I also saw papers, a notebook, some papers, and all of a sudden I realised what that was. I realised that this belonged to a prisoner. And the only thing I asked was "I apologise. Do you know where he resides? He has to take me to the headquarters." He told me, "I'm not a local," and I turned around, went home, and I said to my wife, "Take the child, take your bag and go. Take a taxi and go to Kraljeva Sutjeska, and I will try to do something else and then I will join you later."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you join your family later?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I arrived before my wife. My wife arrived in the evening, and I reached Kraljeva Sutjeska that same day. Only I met a person who would come to visit us. He didn't have a father or mother and he was with me in the detachment. His name was Vito Baric. And I took him with me to accompany me or to guide me to Kraljeva Sutjeska. I didn't know the route, because I hadn't been there before. But before I met him, Vito, I didn't dare go by the hotel. I didn't dare take the highway. I passed the electrical power station, and then I reached the highway there. I went to Visoko --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, can I interrupt you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber why you say that you didn't dare go by the hotel, you didn't dare pass there. Could you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Well, you see, if a deputy commander is arrested, what would happen to me then? So I knew immediately if a deputy commander with official documents - he even had an official pistol - if he can be arrested, then you can imagine what would happen to me. So I didn't dare, because they could have intercepted me there, asked for my ID, and of course I would have ended up there. I would have even fared worse, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said you were on your way to Kraljeva Sutjeska. Could you tell us when you got there.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I got there in the afternoon. It's quite a long way. I went on foot and I took roundabout routes. I arrived in the afternoon, because Francika Baric, Franjo and -- Francika Baric came with me. He used to be in the military police. I went to see him because I thought it was safer for me to go with him to headquarters. However, when I arrived, Franjo had already left, so I went to see his parents. His parents were there, as well as his brother. I asked where Francika was, and they told me, "He has gone. He heard that something was going on in Kakanj." I told them what I had seen, and I said that my wife would come in the afternoon. I didn't dare go via Visoko, since all this was going on. I reckoned I would find full protection in Kraljeva Sutjeska. There's a monastery there. The Franciscans -- the Franciscan order was there, and historically they were always protected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you went to the monastery?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I didn't enter the monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you arrive at Kraljeva Sutjeska? Did you ever arrive?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I did arrive at Kraljeva Sutjeska. And then Francika's father, they called a neighbour, a lady, Kata Subasic was her name, close to the monastery. And she gave me -- she indicated the basement, which is about some 50 metres from where Francika's father lived. I said that my wife would come. She offered me the top floor too. I said, "I don't need it. I just want to see how I can reach Breza and headquarters." However, I stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your family eventually join you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening, my wife arrived, and the child, our child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 13th of June. On that day, in the morning, around 9.00 or maybe -- I apologise. Let me go back a day. The shelling had already started from the direction of Kakanj, the shelling of surrounding villages around Kraljeva Sutjeska, Tesevo, and other villages whose name I didn't know, a Nora was shelling. It's a far -- long-range artillery weapon, and there were mortars as well. And in the evening, women and children fled from Tesevo up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, would that be the 12th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: The 12th, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: They had found accommodation in a large house. There was no one living in it because the owners, they were brothers, I think, in Germany, and we shared a fence. On the ground floor was a large room that was intended as a workshop, and the women went into that premise, business premise. In the morning, about 9.00, shooting could be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would this be the morning of the 13th of June now?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes, the 13th of June, in the morning. Shooting could be heard. And I went outside to see what was happening, and just then from the direction of Tesevo across a small river a group appeared, a large group of soldiers, shooting. Some were going up towards the road, which led to Vares. There's a tunnel up there, and they were climbing up the hill. Later I saw what their intention was. It was not just an intention. It was what they achieved, that is, to block the road. And they came across the river shooting all the while and shouting, "Allah-U-Ekber." And they surrounded these houses, the surrounding houses, and these women and myself. I showed them my army ID card. He didn't even look at it. He just put it in his pocket. And they shepherded us all into this business premise of this house. And in this premises, I was there among the men; Francika's father, a disabled son, another man, an older man that I didn't know; and two young men of about 15 or 16. All the others, more than 50 persons, were all women and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, would you be able to describe for the Trial Chamber what these soldiers looked like? Could you assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: It was a special unit, I know, because they were wearing bulletproof vests, they had real uniforms, as we would say, and they had all the appropriate weaponry, so that, compared with other soldiers, people knew who were special forces or elite forces. I also saw the insignia of the army. There was a young woman inside who recognised one of them as a school friend, and it was thanks to him -- one wanted to shoot with a rifle grenade, but he took it from him and forced him outside. And he said to us, "Don't be afraid. No one will hurt you. Only if we're attacked by your combatants we will force you in front of us so that we can pull out." They went out --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain for the Trial Chamber when you say "army," which army are you speaking about? You said you were able to recognise the insignia of the army. Which army?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. From this house, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this house that you were housed in, did you leave to go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: First they forced us all not to the first floor but to the attic. We weren't allowed to take anything with us. They shoved us into two small rooms, and there was just enough room to stand, and we spent about an hour there. Then they chased us out of those rooms, downstairs, and they took us across the road to another house. But all the things were left behind, all our bags. Usually women were carrying bags with their most valuable things, their most valuable belongings. And in that house there was a corridor, one room to one side, and one to the other. And they pushed us inside. They pulled down the blinds. They designated two women to bring water for the children at 1.00. I remember that very well. And then they left. We were there. We didn't know what to do or what to expect. We couldn't see anything, what was going on. We could hear shooting around us. One woman close to the blind, she raised it and looked out and didn't see anyone. The two young men of 15 or 16 were taken away by them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, did you do anything with your family then? When these soldiers left, did you do anything with your family? Did you take your family anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When we saw there were no soldiers around us, then we took the -- we used the windows facing the hills to get out, all of us. We got out slowly and started uphill. It's a steep hill. Maybe it's about 7 to 8 hundred metres to the top. And we somehow managed to get there through the woods. We reached a meadow near a big transformer station. Then I looked down. Below us were the fields where there were many, many people by then. Throughout that period, one could see the smoke from Kakanj, one could hear shooting. We came down the slope again and joined this host of people, this large group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What area would that be?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: This is Kraljeva Sutjeska, Poljane, the area is called. There's a small field, the polje, and by the end of that field it's called Poljane. Kraljeva Sutjeska is the whole area, however part of it is known as Poljane. It was about 300 metres from the monastery perhaps. And then these people - and I was with them, as well as my family - some had come there in cars, in tractors. There were even trucks. There was even a bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, did you eventually end up in a particular area?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. When these people started burning their property, the cars and things, then the column headed towards Vares. There was about 10.000 people, and I joined the column. We had to pass through territory held by the Serb army - it was called Pernice - in order to reach Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you stay in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: Yes. I reached Vares, and I stayed there. I got in touch with headquarters. They wrote me a letter saying that if I could, I could help the families - and there were about ten Croatian families who were with us in the army - and that I should try and help them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go anywhere else from Vares?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I then, together with these families, managed to find a small tractor with four wheels. The headquarters were waiting with a bus at the border between the HVO and the army. And from there they took us and took us to Breza, where our brigade headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for how long did you live in Breza?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I stayed in Breza until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go to after Breza?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: When I got the appropriate decision and a passport from the Ministry of Defence, I left Breza for Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you live at present, Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO BOROVCANIN
utterances.text: I am living in Germany now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before starting the cross-examination, we are going to have a break. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But just two small questions,

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: of the 126th Mountain Brigade. What was your rank? Were you an ordinary foot soldier? What was your rank?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I had no rank. I was a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a military uniform? Did you have a weapon, insignia?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I had a weapon, a rifle, until 1993. After that I did other jobs as required, but they did not require a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You explained to us that at a certain point in time you saw close to the Sretno Motel an officer who, according to you, had bodyguards. When you saw him, were you in military uniform or in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: At the time, I put on the top part of my uniform, that is, the jacket, because I was at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There's another point to clear up: You told us at the beginning that you were Serb.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you joined the 126th Brigade, which belonged to the 1st Corps, were there Serbs, Croats, Muslims in the 126th Brigade? Who were the members of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Before the brigade was formed, our detachment consisted of three companies: One was the HVO company of the Croatian Defence Council; two companies were Korita and Solakovici. So that apart from me, there were no other Serbs. But there were Croats up until August 1992, when that company -- the HVO company -- was disbanded, and 12 of us, Croats and myself, remained in the detachment. Tone Baric stayed on, who was deputy commander; Ilko Baric, who was assistant chief of staff; Francika, Franjo; Kadar, Braco; Zoka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were the only Serb with Croats.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I was the only Serb, and the others were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were Muslims too?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the question that comes to mind: Who was the enemy?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I was a volunteer there. I was the only Serb in the detachment and later on in the brigade. And in our brigade - the rest had fled or left, I don't know how to put it - there were 12 Croats that stayed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. behind, whereas all the others were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you say that you were in an area in which the 3rd Corps was also present. So you were deployed in the same geographic area. But you were deployed against whom?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Against the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's quarter to 4.00. We're now going to have the break. And we will resume in 25 minutes' time at ten past 4.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We shall now resume. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Cross-examined by Ms. Residovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Borovcanin. My name is Edina Residovic. I represent General Hadzihasanovic. I'm going to ask you to answer a few questions. I believe that these questions are important for the defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear a noise. Papers are being shuffled. And I don't know whether it's the interpreters who do that. Thank you. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, I am going to start with some questions that follow from the questions put to you by the Presiding Judge. Is it true that the Territorial Defence, and later on the BH Army, was actually a multi-ethnic army and that the deputy commander of the Main Staff at that time when you were a member of that army was a Serb, General Jovan Divjak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, is that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the Prosecutor's question, you answered that you currently reside in Germany. Can you please tell me whether you reside in Germany only temporarily or have you regulated your status in Germany.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I reside in Germany only temporarily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were born in February 1940; is that true?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A person who would be ten years your junior or ten years your senior, you wouldn't be in the position to say that that person is of the same age.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In everyday life, if we say that somebody is of our age, we imply that that person was born either the same year as we or one or two years earlier or later; is that true? If somebody were born ten years after or ten years before, you wouldn't say of that person that he was your age; is that true?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: It depends on how they look. There are persons who look younger and who are nevertheless older and vice versa. For example, somebody will say, "I am 70, and others will say I am 50." I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on I'll ask about that. I was just asking it is not customary to say about somebody who is ten years younger or older that they are of our own age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: It depends on how they look. In 1992, I didn't have a single white hair on my head. A year or two later I had a head full of white hair. I changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In -- where we come from, people are rather tall. If somebody was 170 centimetres tall, we wouldn't say that he was tall. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No, we wouldn't say that. I am 181, and I'm tall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were 170, would you be tall then?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Well, that is also a certain height. It's very difficult for me to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If somebody weighed 65 kilos and he was a man, would we say that he was a strong, sturdily built person?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No, we wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me ask you something that arises from your testimony. So far I've only asked you general questions. Is it true that before your today's testimony you also gave a statement to the Prosecutors of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since some of my questions will arise from the statement, I would kindly ask for the witness to be provided with a copy of his statement in B/C/S and in English as well. You can also give it to the other participants; however, I don't think I will tender any of the parts of this statement into evidence. But it would be useful for all of us to have it in front of us at the moment when I put my questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can look at the statement in B/C/S. Is it true that you gave this statement on 17th September 2001?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 4, the last paragraph on that page. Here you give a detailed description of Enver Hadzihasanovic. You say that you think that he was of about your age, that he was about 1.80 metres tall, and that he is of strong build. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes. I would repeat the same thing today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: May I interrupt, please. Nowhere in my examination-in-chief did I ask the witness about any description with respect to the accused Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've said, Mr. President, I would like to use parts of the statement in order to check the credibility and I am not going to base my questions on the questions put to the witness by my learned friend. I'm going to use another basis for checking the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the questions put to you by my learned friend. You said that on the 1st of May, 1992 you had joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which later on became the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the then-constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was the only armed force in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you were born in Olovo, at that time you resided in Ilijas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, I resided in Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since at the time Serbs had proclaimed Ilijas a part of the Serbian Autonomous Province, most, if not all citizens who were not Serbs were either expelled or had left the territory under the control of the Serb forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your own words, you were a volunteer, you abandoned the area, and you decided to become a member of the Territorial Defence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your detachment, Korita, as well as some other detachments which existed at the time in the course of 1993 became integral parts of the brigades of the army which was being established at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your brigade was part of the 1st Corps of the BH Army whose headquarters were in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I said that this is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your superior command was the command of the 1st Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, as a matter of fact, in the course of 1993, because of the blockade of Sarajevo, some of the units of the 1st Corps were also active in the territories covered by other corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 1st Corps was in Sarajevo. Sarajevo was blocked at the time. Some of the units and brigades of the 1st Corps were active outside of the boundaries of the city of Sarajevo. Sometimes in the areas that belonged to the zone of responsibility of other corps. For example, some units were active in the territory of the 3rd Corps, some in the territory of the 4th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, part of this is correct. However, units of the 1st Corps, as far as I know - and I know about our area of responsibility - were in the zone of the command of the 3rd Corps. But they only arrived once the tunnel had been dug. They arrived in the area of Vares and I believe that it was the 105th and some other brigades. I know that they arrived in the vicinity of Vares.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this did happen for some specific reasons that were prevalent during that war.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You as a member of the army at that time were aware of the fact that in late 1992 and beginning 1993 in the general area where your unit also was a lot of refugees arrived from the areas which were under the control of the Serb forces and later on under the control of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there were refugees from that area, mostly in Breza, Kakanj, and in Visoko. From our area, some Croats also went to Kiseljak and further on. I don't know where they went at that time. But in any case, there were a lot of displaced persons in the area of Kakanj, Breza, Visoko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that at that time a lot of refugees who came after the fall of Jajce arrived in that area carrying their own arms and that there were a lot of self-organised groups which were active in that general area?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: In the area where I was - and that was from Naborzici [phoen] - if you have a map, I can show you - towards Visoko, Breza, and Kakanj, I didn't see any other. And I claim that there weren't any such groups besides the BH Army and the HVO. As I've already said, there was also MOS --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: HOS?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No, MOS. Some said that the abbreviation stood for the Muslim Liberation Alliance, or something like that. I don't know what the abbreviation stood for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that some of these units were mostly formed in various villages close to the religious buildings and under the influence of some religious leaders? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: That was not the case in our area. A detachment was formed, but there was no priest or hodza involved. A detachment was formed. The 1st Detachment, and later on --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You mentioned the MOS and some other forces. Do you know anything about them? How were they formed? If you don't know, just say you don't know. That is also an answer.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is an answer; however, I wouldn't -- I wouldn't know who created those forces and why, who established them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your family was for a while in Breza and later on you moved to Kakanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No. My family was in Kakanj, and then when we went from Kakanj to Kraljeva Sutjeska and then to Vares. Then we arrived in Breza, where we stayed until 1995. That's how we closed the full refugee circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Kakanj, there was the Municipal Staff of the Territorial Defence of the BH Army and the majority of the local population, especially Muslims, were mobilised into the BH Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although you were in Kakanj, you were up to the end of May -- that is, 20 May 1993 -- at the front line most of the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: It depended on the situation. I would occasionally be on the front line for ten days in a row. Sometimes, when it was calm and peaceful, I would go to help the refugees to transport food for them. That was -- that's how I was more useful than if I had been sitting up there. So sometimes I would be on the front line for ten days, sometimes for seven days. It would depend on the shifts and on the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that in Kakanj you lived in Povezice, in the house of a local Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you were in the street the name of which was the Fraternity and Unity Street, which belonged to that neighbourhood of Povezice.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: The street name was Povezice. I never heard of this other name that you mentioned. I never heard of this other name. I know that Povezice was Povezice and that was the name of the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That street or that neighbourhood -- according to me, although you say it was just the name of the street -- on one side of the street there was a row of terrace houses and on the other side of the railroad there was another block of apartments.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, on the other side of the railroad in front of the motel there was another block of apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is an embankment there and there still is, and from the terraced houses, because of the embankment and the block of apartments across the railroad you could see nothing but the roof of the motel. You couldn't see the entrance.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I couldn't see the entrance, because it was -- the vision was blocked. But it is not true that I could see nothing but the roof. I could also see the windows on the upper floors. I couldn't see the basement and the entrance, but I could see the rooms and the windows on the upper floors, as well as the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not the only refugee family in that street. In the row of terraced houses, there were a number of refugees who had arrived from Romanija, Sokolac, and from other areas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you will remember that the families of Ivica and Emina Komljen; Pero and Rosa Banovac, Petla Batlavic [phoen], his sons Marko and Ilija, and some other families resided there at the same time like the Penjic family; is that correct family is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: In that row of houses, as far as the refugees are concerned, I didn't know any refugee. I didn't know them because I didn't know this area of Kakanj. I knew Kakanj as such very well. I was the president of the Society of Private Entrepreneurs, but I didn't know this particular neighbourhood. I knew by sight some people. I saw Mr. Hadzihasanovic's family. There was his wife and two children, the son and the daughter. There were some other families whom I didn't know. I didn't know where they were from. I was not interested in that. So in that part there were not so many refugees as you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the Prosecution's question, you said that at that time in 1993 the 3rd Corps was established. Is it true that its base was in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that the first commander of the 3rd Corps was General Alagic, who was followed by General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please be more precise and tell us up to when was General Alagic the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't be more precise. They -- when I was in Kakanj, there were no ranks. He was not a general. They referred to him as a commander. When one replaced the other and what their positions in the Main Staff was -- I really don't know what was the situation in the 3rd Corps. I can only tell you about the things that I witnessed and where I was. I can tell you about any detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. But in any case --

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I can also tell you about my Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since this is correct that there were no ranks, you know that the first commander of the 3rd Corps was Alagic and then that he was followed by Hadzihasanovic as commander. You've already said that to -- in reply to the Prosecutor's question. A little while ago, Mr. Borovcanin, you said that in this row of terraced houses, in one of these houses there was the wife and children of Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes. This was a couple of houses further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that morning that you were talking about, up to that morning you never knew which house this was. So on the morning of the 20th, you asked somebody to point the Hadzihasanovic family's house to you.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I knew these houses, because you could see them. This is not far from where I was, maybe three or four houses further away. I knew that one of these three or four houses was his house. I knew that it was there, because I would see him and I would see his wife, his cows walking around. I was not interested in who was walking where and who was there. I minded my own business. I had my family and my commitments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, Enver Hadzihasanovic's family, together with other refugees, was living in a still-not-completed house which had been abandoned by a Serb family; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had abandoned it and how they were living in it. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that in this unfinished house there were 11 people living on the ground floor, 4 refugee families, you will agree with me that that is correct?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No, I won't. I don't remember that anywhere in Kakanj at the time that I was there that there were in a house in the area I was in that was inhabited by four or five families. I can't agree with that, and I'm afraid I can't even believe it. You would have to convince me of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You personally never entered that house, did you?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I know -- I know that in front there were some Serbs; to the right, there was Jelic houses. And therefore I know how it was. In Dumanac [phoen], a little further on, there was a friend of mine -- Ferid, his name was. He was also with me on the front. But there, where I lived, I can claim that there was no house inhabited by four families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 11 persons.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I didn't count.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, please: You never personally met Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you testified, when you saw that he had come to visit his wife and children, you would always see him alone. You never saw him with an escort.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: He didn't have a military escort. When he came in a car, once I saw him in a jeep - I don't know who was inside. I wouldn't stand watching to see who was passing by. I didn't see him having a military escort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said that on the 18th of May, 1993, you saw a van with these soldiers with green bands round their heads.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: On the 18th, they arrived at the motel up there, at the Sretno Motel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And on that day, you didn't see Enver Hadzihasanovic anywhere, did you?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him that day. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, the conclusion as to why these men had arrived was your own assumption. You had no information about that, did you?

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: I didn't have anyone to get information from. But knowing the area; knowing the reality; and how and what things were happening and how a combat unit acts; and that the police would come to the Sretno Motel; and that a unit was located there -- at first, I thought it might be because of conflicts in Central Bosnia, that perhaps some kind of security had arrived for Hadzihasanovic because a conflict had broken out between the Croats and the army and in Kakanj there was the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Borovcanin, you told me a moment ago that in addition to the HVO there was the Territorial Defence and units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the same time.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes. There was a special unit located up there, a special unit of the police, in the centre up there. I know some men. I know the commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among these refugees that you saw, you said, seeing some in the Povezice neighbourhood there were some who were members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina like yourself.

utterances.speaker: I didn't quite understand.  You told us that you were a member
utterances.text: Yes. Across the road from my place there was Tone Baric. And next to me, the house next to where I was, in the direction of Kakanj - I've forgotten his name - but he was in Tale's detachment. We knew each other very well. His little son had a heart attack and died, et cetera. Everyone knows about that.
